avatars.name: The Late Starter
avatars.tagline: A man who never really got going with dating and now feels behind everyone he knows.
avatars.who: A single man, usually late 20s to early 40s (with an older tail in his 50s), who has never had an official girlfriend or whose longest relationship lasted a few months. He gets few or no matches, ends up in the friend zone, or gets first dates that never turn into second ones, and he freezes or overthinks around women he likes. Many work hands-on or hourly jobs, live in small towns or rural areas, and are in therapy for anxiety, depression or old family wounds. He books the call because he has run out of ideas on his own and wants someone to show him, step by step, what he is doing wrong.

profile.relationship_history: Never had a committed relationship, or only short flings and 'almosts'. Some were burned once (cheated on, an abusive partner, a one-sided friendship) and have been single for years since.
profile.work_and_money: Mixed and often thin: tradesmen, techs, hospitality, freelancers, people between jobs or with no income, plus a few salaried IT or office workers. Money is the most common blocker; several had no savings, no credit or under a thousand dollars available.
profile.apps_and_tried: Hinge, Tinder or Facebook Dating with few or no replies; some have stopped using apps. Tried therapy, books, YouTube or pickup content, friends reviewing profiles, speed dating, and in a couple of cases a previous dating coach that did not help.

goals: A first real, committed relationship that leads to marriage and kids
Confidence to start conversations and approach women without freezing
An honest outside read, ideally from a woman, on what he is doing wrong
Move from first dates and friend zone to a second date and real interest
Stop feeling behind his friends and family
Someone to come home to instead of evenings alone
pains: Few or no matches, and women go quiet once he asks them out
Stuck in the friend zone or first dates that fizzle with no explanation
Anxiety, overthinking and freezing around women he is attracted to
Low self-worth: feels like a loser, not marriage material, or too late
Lonely evenings and few places to meet women, especially in small towns
Embarrassment at family events and watching friends get married

objections.what_it_really_means: Often a real cash limit, not a value doubt. He may have no income, no savings or no credit, and nobody asked before the pitch.
objections.quote: $7,200 is a lot. The money is stretched thin at the moment.

objections.what_it_really_means: He is doing per-session maths against cheap coaches or therapy because he does not yet see what the three months buys him.
objections.quote: at $7,200 for three months, that's over $2,000 a month. And if I only meet with her four times a month, that's what, $400 or $500 a session? So that's a lot.

objections.what_it_really_means: He has been told yes and then let down before, so he needs time away from pressure to trust his own decision.
objections.quote: I don't want to sign or pay anything today. I want to have a little bit of time to think over this first.

objections.what_it_really_means: Money is fine; the fear is paying for a second coach who also gives generic advice and no result.
objections.quote: I'm okay financially, and I can afford what she asked me, but, like, as I said, my previous… dating coach experience, I'm kind of more cautious.

avatars.what_they_need_vs_what_we_sell: He needs basic skills and reps: profile and photos, how to open and keep a conversation going, how to show romantic interest, and steady encouragement while his confidence builds. The program covers that well (Reset, Inner Game, Read and Lead), but at $7,200 it is priced above what many of these men can pay, so the bi-weekly $3,600 tier is the realistic fit and should be the recommendation when money is tight.

Feels behind: friends married, family asking, 'I'm getting old'

how_to_sell: Qualify money gently before the pitch; many of these men cannot invest four figures, and finding out after the price wastes the call

avatars.name: The Rusty Returner
avatars.tagline: A divorced or widowed man in his 50s or 60s who was good at this once and now feels lost on the apps.
avatars.who: An older man, usually divorced (sometimes widowed or grieving), who has been out of the dating world for years or has drifted from one wrong relationship to the next. He is often successful or comfortable (business owner, lawyer, pilot, tech) but some are on pensions, two jobs or fixed incomes. The apps feel like a minefield of fakes, scams and flakes, he gets few replies or one date that goes nowhere, and he worries about seeming too old or creepy. He is on the call because he is lonely, the clock feels real, and he wants a guide for a game whose rules changed.

profile.age: 41 to 72, most in their mid 50s to 60s
profile.relationship_history: Long marriage ended in divorce (or a spouse died), then years of little or no dating, or a string of on-and-off relationships with women who were not a match or wanted money.
profile.work_and_money: Split. Some are secure (retired business owners, lawyers, Google, pilots) and the money is not the issue; others are on pensions, fixed incomes or rebuilding after a failed business and are heavily price-anchored.
profile.kids: Often grown or teenage kids; a few still raising young children after divorce.
profile.apps_and_tried: Match, Tinder, Facebook Dating, eHarmony, Christian Mingle, Hinge. Many have already paid for matchmaking or another coach (including in-person or pickup-style coaches) and feel it did not deliver.

goals: A long-term partner for the next 20 or 30 years, someone who has his back
Get his confidence and old self back with women
Know where to meet the right women offline and which apps to use
Read women's intentions early and spot fakes, scams and gold-diggers
A better profile, photos and messages that actually get replies
Companionship: travel, dinners, someone beside him at the end of the day
pains: Apps full of fake profiles, bots, scams and women who will not meet
Few replies or one date that never becomes a second
Loneliness and the fear of dying alone
Feels too old, worries about seeming creepy or being written off
Keeps choosing or attracting the wrong women
Already paid for matchmaking or coaching that did not work

avatars.name: The Almost-Boyfriend

avatars.who: A single professional man in his early to mid 30s (finance, sales, tech, media, a family business) who has no trouble getting dates. His relationships stay undefined for months, end at the three or four month mark, or he picks the wrong woman and gives too much. Career took priority for years, friends are now getting married, and he has started to feel the clock. He books the call because he is self-aware, often in therapy, and wants a practical outside read on why nothing becomes official.

profile.relationship_history: Plenty of dating, a few undefined or short relationships, sometimes one long relationship that ended. Never or rarely in a committed, defined relationship he chose.
profile.work_and_money: Salaried professionals or business heirs who can usually invest four figures, though some cap what they will spend on 'help they don't really need'.
profile.apps_and_tried: Mostly Hinge. Tried therapy, books, podcasts, Kim's content; some looked at matchmakers.

Move a connection from undefined to an exclusive relationship

Choose the right partner instead of the next good one

Women can't tell if he wants friendship or a relationship
Validation-seeking and overanalysing when she pulls back
Years of career focus, now friends are married and he feels left behind

avatars.name: The Clock-Watcher
avatars.tagline: A successful woman in her 30s or 40s who keeps picking unavailable men while the family clock ticks.
avatars.who: A single professional woman, often a therapist, counsellor or corporate or military professional, from her early 30s to late 40s. She dates, but her relationships stall at two or three months, turn into situationships, or end with an avoidant man disappearing, and she wonders what is wrong with her. Many want a child and feel time running out; several are the last single friend in their group. She is on the call because she has done the therapy and the reading and wants practical, directive dating guidance.

profile.work_and_money: Professionals with income (therapists, military, corporate, finance). Most can invest, but some are cash-tight, self-employed or wary of financing interest.
profile.kids: Mostly no kids; many want one soon.

Practical guidance on the 'sport' of dating, not more theory

Long situationships with men who will not commit

avatars.name: The One-Situation Fixer
avatars.tagline: Someone who wants a verdict on one person (an ex, a crush, a new partner), not a dating program.
avatars.who: Usually a man (from late 20s to mid 50s) whose whole focus is a single person: an ex he wants back, a crush who is hot and cold, a woman still living with her ex-husband, or a new girlfriend he is afraid of scaring off. He overthinks, ruminates and wants someone to decode her signals and tell him what to do. He often says outright that he dates fine otherwise. He books the call wanting clarity on that one situation, and the application usually says so.

profile.kids: Mostly no kids; a divorced dad of a young child is the exception.

avatars.what_they_need_vs_what_we_sell: They want a quick, specific answer about one person, which the program does not sell and coaching cannot honestly promise (especially getting an ex back). Reps end up improvising one-off sessions to fit the ask; the only sellable version is reframing the call around the pattern behind the situation (overthinking, communication, choosing unavailable people) and the next relationship.
how_to_spot: Application names one person or one breakup ('getting her back', 'mixed signals', 'a woman I've had a crush on')
Talks about one woman for most of the first five minutes
Says he gets dates fine or is not looking for general dating help
Uses words like clarity, signals, decode, reach out, closure
how_to_sell: Set the frame early: Kim does not get exes back; she fixes the pattern so the next relationship works

If the pattern is not there, release him kindly instead of selling an improvised single session

universal_objections.insight: The most common objection on calls and in texts. Most often it lands because money was never asked about before the pitch, so the price exposes a budget wall that discovery could have found in minutes.
universal_objections.quote: I just, I can't afford it right now is really what it comes down to.

universal_objections.insight: Many buyers across avatars have a personal rule against same-call decisions. Long pushes after this turn warm leads cold; a belief check and a firm next step work better.
universal_objections.quote: I feel like I need time to process that. I'm not like, I'm not balking at, I am balking, but just processing.

universal_objections.insight: Prospects ask for guarantees or proof. Reps answer with partner-rate claims the playbook forbids; the honest answer is the process and visible change.
universal_objections.quote: am I willing to pay that amount of money to hopefully get, you know, this end result, like if it was guaranteed, then I would do it.

universal_objections.insight: A frequent ask is to meet Kim or pay for one session before committing. There is no sanctioned answer, so reps invent $1,000 calls and deposits that become the product.
universal_objections.quote: is there a way where you do like you pay for the first session and just see like get the feel for it first before you commit to the $7,000 or it might be?

universal_objections.insight: Therapy (often covered by insurance or work benefits) is the main alternative, especially for women. The pitch needs a clear line between insight and directive dating guidance.
universal_objections.quote: Getting a therapist is a cheaper option at this point

universal_objections.insight: Some prospects decide to step back from dating to work on themselves; pushing time scarcity rarely moves them.
universal_objections.quote: I've kind of decided that the time and effort I've spent dating these women and pointing towards them, I'm going to put towards myself again.

who_buys: Buyers name a repeating pattern in their own words, have the money or credit to act on the call, and decide alone: professional women around 40 with an unavailable-men or long situationship pattern, men around 30 with good careers whose relationships never become official, a wealthy older divorced man, and younger novices who came warm from Kim's content. They hit a high score on the temperature check before price and their only objection is which tier or how to pay. Non-buyers mostly fall into three groups: people who cannot invest four figures (no income, fixed income, debt, or a few hundred dollars), people who want a single session or a verdict on one person rather than a program, and older sceptics who were burned by a past coach or matchmaker and ask for guarantees. Across all groups the calls that were lost usually had price stated before money was qualified, and then improvised discounts, deposits and financing pushes.
icp_gap: The closing doc describes four segments split evenly by gender, with the successful woman as the achiever and an older divorced woman as the rebuilder. In practice the ad funnel targets men and its applicants skew 55 and over, so most sales calls are with men, many of them older returners on mixed incomes or late-starting novices with little money. A large share of calls fall outside the four segments: men around 30 who date easily but cannot make it official, and people who only want help with one specific person. The people who actually buy are professional women in their late 30s and 40s and men in their 30s with careers, plus the occasional wealthy older man; older women and one-situation callers rarely buy. The sanctioned $3,600 bi-weekly tier matches what many novices and older women can pay, yet it is seldom offered and reps invent cheaper options instead.
